strengths: Studying the WeakS-to-Strong setting is well-motivated and using the proposed Bayesian method here is novel. Furthermore, the expansion to from binary verification tasks to generation is notable since the latter more realistically reflects LLM use cases.

The paper’s proposed method results in notable improvements on the studied tasks, outperforming the individual weak model teachers in isolation and the naive baseline that simply does a weighted average over the standard CE-based losses. I also appreciated the extra ablations the authors ran to verify the importance of certain aspects of their design (e.g., the aux loss, probability estimation for weak sequences and the λ weights across tasks).
Overall, I found the writing to be clear, doing a good job of contextualizing methods/results in terms of prior work.

The paper is the first to successfully extend weak-to-strong to the weaks-to-strong setting. The paper also contains several useful ideas for performing sequence-level training using soft-labels when the student and the teacher have different tokenizers.
The paper is written well and is easy to follow.

The experiments are well structured to answer the central questions posed by the paper, i.e., is weaks-to-strong better than weak-to-strong, and is the proposed method of performing weaks-to-strong training better than naive baselines?
Based on the quality of the experiments and the topic addressed, I believe that a broad community will find the paper useful.
The proposal is simple but works.
They propose a Bayesian WeakS-to-Strong framework that improves weak supervison.(Although I tend to say this improvement is not well-proved).
Extention of Weak-to-Strong framework from text classification to generation tasks.
A method for estimating token-level probabilities is introduced to create soft labels for training robust models.
weaknesses: Certain claims in the manuscript were not as strongly supported by the empirical results; for instance, the improvements obtained from the DPO-based stage weren't too big (i.e., within standard deviations across runs), and the claim about the auxiliary loss improving Bayesian methods.

Consider methods from data programming / programmatic weak supervision (e.g., Snorkel, FlyingSquid) to aggregate the labels generated by different weak models, and discuss this line of work given that they also operate in a setting where the goal is to aggregate multiple weak label sources.
In the related work, the authors mentioned that some previous works (Liu & Asahi, 2024; Sang et al., 2024) tried traditional ensembling methods; perhaps these would also be useful baselines.
It would strengthen the paper if the authors could show similar results on more tasks per category (i.e., classification, generation), as currently the results are limited to one task for each.

The best results rely on the "Fixed Weight" approach which assumes one can accurately estimate the weak model performances; the applicability of this assumption to real superhuman tasks where ground-truth labels are difficult to obtain is unclear.

Given the motivation to consider variation in human opinions, it is unclear how the methods/results would generalize when supervision comes from humans rather than weak models, especially since confidence estimates associated with weak model labels may not exist for human-generated labels.

Some of the design choices are not well justified; for example, the strategy proposed in section 4.1 for sequence-level training using soft labels is unclear why it should work or be optimal, especially regarding handling ambiguous tokenization and word-level alignment between teacher and student models, and the paper lacks analysis of potential error propagation or information loss.

The datasets selected for the classification and generation tasks seem very specific; the lack of diversity (e.g., only SciQ for classification and only SLURP for generation) limits the generalizability and makes it difficult to assess broader applicability to tasks such as text summarization or machine translation.
The motivation for using Dirichlet distribution to model the prior is ambiguous.
The writing for the methodology description is unclear and hard to follow.
The transformations in Equation 3 should be clarified.
What is the definition of $p_k$ in Equation 4?

In Section 4.1, the probability of the target token of the strong model changes after each update of network parameters because $C_s(s_1)$ and $C_s(s_2)$ shift, leading to targets varying along training, likely creating instability or divergence, and recomputing these terms is time-consuming.
All baselines that are naive and very simple algorithms are weak for both classification and generation tasks; stronger baselines should be included for both tasks.
The experiments are not comprehensive: they mainly involve ~1B weak models and a ~7B strong model, making the claim on WeakS-to-Strong slightly overclaimed.
The improvement shown in the experiment is not observable; for example, accuracy 0.843 (baseline) vs 0.850 (WeakS-to-Strong-3) is negligible.
